The Shutdown Breaks Records, the President Breaks With the Courts

A week of hunger politics, election panic, mass pardons, and a president who told his own vice president to say the judiciary was wrong

```markdown This was the week the country's longest government shutdown collided with an election that went badly for the president, and the aftershocks reached nearly every branch of government. By its end, food assistance for 42 million Americans had become the subject of an open standoff between the executive branch and the federal judiciary, voters had delivered a rebuke at the ballot box that the president refused to accept, and the week closed with a mass pardon of allies who had tried to overturn the last election alongside the resignation of a federal judge who said he could no longer stay silent about what he called a weaponized Justice Department.

**The Weekend**

The weekend began with a rupture in the social safety net that had not occurred in 61 years: SNAP benefits lapsed nationwide as the shutdown dragged past its fourth week, with the administration declining to tap emergency reserves that could have kept payments flowing. States scrambled to respond, and a federal judge ordered the administration to use contingency funds — an order met with partial and contested compliance from the outset, setting a pattern that would define the entire week. At the same time, federal courts in five cities — Washington, Portland, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Memphis — ruled against the administration's deployment of National Guard troops in or near American cities, finding violations of federal law, the Tenth Amendment, and the Posse Comitatus Act. Multiple courts, independently, had reached the same conclusion: the domestic use of military force against protest activity exceeded the president's authority.

Against this backdrop, the administration's public posture struck an odd note. Trump posted images of a renovated Kennedy Center and a newly gilded White House bathroom, then traveled to Mar-a-Lago for a 76th golf outing, pushing the term's taxpayer-funded golf costs past $60 million. Overseas, the Defense Department carried out a lethal strike on a boat in the Caribbean, killing three people, and Trump directed preparations for possible military action in Nigeria, threatening to cut off aid or invade over alleged persecution of Christians — all without seeking congressional authorization, even as the 60-day deadline under the War Powers Resolution passed unaddressed. A smaller story emerged from within the FBI, where a career official who oversaw the agency's pilot unit was pushed out after news coverage revealed FBI Director Kash Patel's personal use of a government jet — the third head of that unit removed under his leadership.

**Monday**

The symbolism of institutional priorities sharpened further. Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing, office space used by first ladies since 1942, to make way for a $300 million ballroom — a personal legacy project replacing infrastructure the position had long used for public advocacy. The administration also announced it would send federal election monitors to California and New Jersey ahead of Tuesday's vote, prompting state officials in both to accuse Washington of intimidation and to dispatch their own observers to watch the federal ones. Separately, new reporting sharpened a picture of concentrated wealth and access: Oxfam found the ten richest Americans had gained $698 billion over the past year, while Public Citizen reported that two-thirds of corporate donors to Trump's ballroom project had received $279 billion in federal contracts, with more than a dozen facing suspended enforcement actions. An immigration judge, meanwhile, denied bond to a detained photojournalist over religious social media posts, citing a statute against endorsing terrorism — a ruling that raised First Amendment concerns about treating protected speech as grounds for detention. In one piece of good news for institutional guardrails, the White House withdrew its nominee to lead the Office of Special Counsel after Republican senators balked at disclosures that he had described having "a Nazi streak."

**Tuesday**

Tuesday was the most consequential single day of the week. Voters delivered sweeping wins for Democrats, including a 14-point victory for Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey's governor's race and passage of California's Proposition 50 redistricting measure. Bomb threats disrupted polling places in New Jersey and Virginia. Rather than accept the results, Trump posted baseless claims that the election was "rigged," and press secretary Karoline Leavitt echoed unsubstantiated fraud allegations from the White House podium. Trump went further, calling any Jewish voter who supported New York mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani "stupid," while Rep. Andy Ogles posted racist and false content about Mamdani alongside 9/11 imagery and threats to pursue his removal from office under the 14th Amendment.

The same day, the Justice Department indicted former FBI Director James Comey for lying to Congress and obstruction, and New York Attorney General Letitia James on bank fraud charges — prosecutions that followed explicit public demands from Trump and drew criticism from more than 100 former DOJ officials as vindictive and thinly evidenced. John Bolton was separately charged with mishandling classified information. On the SNAP front, despite the earlier court order, Trump declared that food assistance would remain withheld until Democrats agreed to "open up government," while Senate Republicans blocked a resolution to fully fund the program. The shutdown itself reached its 35th day, tying the record set during Trump's first term, with a newly elected House member unable to be sworn in or vote. Separately, armed ICE agents arrested a US citizen father at a Los Angeles Home Depot and drove off with his one-year-old daughter still in the car, leaving her grandmother to retrieve her hours later.

**Wednesday**

The Supreme Court heard arguments over whether Trump's sweeping tariffs were lawful under emergency economic powers, with justices across the ideological spectrum — including Chief Justice Roberts — expressing skepticism toward the administration's claim that the tariffs were "regulatory" rather than a form of taxation reserved to Congress. California Republicans, meanwhile, filed a federal lawsuit within hours of Proposition 50's passage, seeking to block the newly approved congressional maps on claims a state official's team called certain to fail. Trump, in a speech and a private breakfast with Republican senators, blamed the party's election losses on the shutdown and pressed them to eliminate the Senate filibuster, engaging in a heated exchange with Senator Lindsey Graham. Steve Bannon urged federal agencies to investigate Mamdani's citizenship and suggested the DOJ seek a court order delaying California's new maps. And in the Comey case, a federal magistrate rebuked the Justice Department's approach as "indict first, investigate later," ordering prosecutors to turn over grand jury materials.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought some of the week's sharpest judicial findings. Judge McConnell ruled that the administration had defied the earlier SNAP order, withholding benefits "for political reasons" — citing Trump's own social media posts as evidence — and ordered full payment by Friday; the administration immediately appealed. The Supreme Court's conservative majority, separately, reinstated a policy requiring passports to reflect sex assigned at birth, blocking transgender and non-binary applicants from accurate identification over a dissent from the Court's three liberal justices. In Chicago, a federal judge found that Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino had lied under oath about being struck by a rock before deploying tear gas on protesters, with video showing he was hit only after using the chemical agent; the same judge issued a broad injunction limiting crowd-control force against demonstrators, clergy, and journalists. Video also surfaced of ICE agents forcibly detaining a daycare worker in front of children during an operation the agency said targeted a vehicle. Economic data added to the week's unease: October saw 153,074 job cuts, a 183 percent jump from September, alongside a $125 billion emergency liquidity injection by the Federal Reserve into the banking system over five days.

**Friday**

The week closed with a capstone act: Trump signed Proclamation 10989, granting broad federal pardons to 77 people connected to the effort to overturn the 2020 election, including Rudy Giuliani, Mark Meadows, and fake electors from seven states. The pardons were announced via social media at a time apparently chosen to minimize coverage, and they left pending state prosecutions untouched. On the same day, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson issued an administrative stay blocking full distribution of SNAP benefits after the administration sought Supreme Court intervention, and Vice President Vance publicly called the underlying court order "absurd," asserting the executive branch would decide unilaterally what compliance meant — a remarkable statement given that a federal judge had, only a day earlier, found the administration in defiance of a court order.

Also on Friday, Judge Mark Wolf, a Reagan appointee with fifty years on the bench, resigned, saying he could no longer stay silent about the administration's targeting of political opponents while sparing its donors and allies from scrutiny. The Senate voted 49-51 against a war-powers resolution that would have required congressional approval for continued strikes in Venezuela, even as a federal judge issued a final order permanently barring National Guard deployment to Portland, finding no credible evidence of violence to justify it. In a smaller but telling footnote, Trump's trade office announced a deal cutting Switzerland's tariff rate from 39 to 15 percent, days after Swiss business leaders had presented him with a gold clock and bar of gold at the White House. And at more than 100 universities, students and faculty organized a coordinated day of action opposing federal funding conditions tied to ideological compliance — the first large-scale, nationally coordinated response from higher education to that pressure.

Taken as a whole, the week traced two threads that ran in parallel rather than merging into a single story. One was a test of whether the executive would obey the judiciary at all: a program serving 42 million people became the arena in which courts repeatedly found the administration in violation of the law, only for the administration to appeal, delay, and ultimately secure a stay that left the underlying dispute unresolved. The other was a president's response to a decisive electoral defeat — not through concession or recalibration, but through unfounded claims of fraud, attacks on the loyalty of a religious minority, and pressure on his own party to dismantle a legislative safeguard in the name of political survival. That these threads culminated, on the same Friday, in pardons erasing federal accountability for a prior attempt to subvert an election and in a judge's public resignation over the politicization of prosecution, left little room for the week to be read as a series of unconnected events. It was, instead, a compressed record of the strain that direct confrontation between the executive branch and the other institutions of American government can place on all of them at once. ```
